groups.title: Social standing
groups.intro: Social Status and how characters of different standing deal with one another.

entries.title: The Cost of Breaking Convention
entries.summary: Optional guideline that penalizes a magus who dresses above his station, trails armed men, or flaunts his familiar in public when dealing with mundanes, unless he makes an effort to follow convention.
quotes: he suffers an additional –1 social interaction penalty

entries.title: The Gratitude System
entries.summary: An optional structured advancement system in which characters earn Gratitude points from their lord for service beyond their station, then redeem them for higher office, land or goods. The text lists how many points different kinds of story outcome are worth.
quotes: Characters earn Gratitude points when they perform a service to their lord that is beyond that required by their station.
If the story requires the character to complete a feat that will be widely renowned for its difficulty

entries.title: Advancement Requirements Table
entries.summary: A table of what a character needs, and what it costs the granting lord, to move between ranks such as serf, freeman, knight, bacheler, landed noble, banneret and baron, or to take an office. Notes explain how many heroic or exceptional services a promotion normally takes.
quotes: Gratitude 10, marriage to suitable heiress, or claiming land during war, or being offered land that has returned to the lord.
Appointment as an officer to Greater Baron or higher requires Gratitude 10, Landed Noble (at minimum), Reputation for loyalty to the lord, vacancy in the office, and office-specific traits.

related.text: Chapter Three: A Comparison of Titles

groups.title: Nobility and feudal life
groups.intro: Titles, vassals, retinues, offices and the gratitude system.

entries.title: Retinue
entries.summary: Explains the four parts of a magnate's household (family, military, clerical and menial) and gives typical household sizes by noble rank, useful for sizing a lord's following.
quotes: Speaking loosely, the household of a lord of the manor averages 10, that of a landed knight 16, that of a banneret 24, that of a baron 40, and that of an earl 140.

entries.title: A Random Method of Death
entries.summary: An optional method for secretly rolling the age at which non-player characters die, so that lines of inheritance take unexpected turns, with adjustments for wartime. The text warns it is harsher than the standard aging rules.
quotes: Assume that any child has a 25% chance of dying of natural causes before adulthood is reached.
assume a death age of 6 simple dice + 20 years

entries.title: A Random Method of Life
entries.summary: Companion method for a character waiting to inherit: check each person ahead of them for a new legitimate child, then check each child for a random age of death.
quotes: Then roll a die for each, assuming that on average half of them do have a child.

entries.title: Military
entries.summary: Covers the household knights (the mesnie) of a lord, the status of a bacheler and a carissimus, and how mesnie loyalty works in practice. Includes Intelligence + Intrigue rolls to recall a mesnie's common features or find a lord who favors a skill.
quotes: A character may make an Intelligence + Intrigue roll against an Ease Factor of 6 to recall if the mesnie members of a lord with whom he is interacting have a common feature.
A knight becomes a bacheler by being offered a place in a mesnie.

entries.title: Offices
entries.summary: Explains what an officer of a lord is, how officers differ from hereditary vassals, what their underlings will and will not do, and that characters built as officers need the Temporal Influence Virtue. The individual offices that follow are descriptive.
quotes: Characters designed as officers need the Temporal Influence Virtue.

entries.title: Money
entries.summary: The taxes vassals owe their liege: relief on inherited land (with the four graces that make it affordable) and discretionary aids paid on occasions such as knighting an heir or ransom.
quotes: it is capped at five pounds per manor, or 100 pounds for greater barons, regardless of actual income
In England, a lord owes approximately one year's income to his liege on the assumption of his title.

entries.title: Warriors
entries.summary: Military service owed by vassals: knights per manor, optional extra forces, peasant levies and what infantry are good for, and the limited number of days of service per year that vary by kingdom.
quotes: vassals are required to provide their lord with the service of one knight for per manor that their fief contained at the time it was originally granted
Assume that a powerful landowner must provide, at minimum, 20 knights when called to war.
In England this is 40 days, in Sicily 60.

entries.title: Scutage
entries.summary: The money a vassal may pay in place of sending knights to a war, why both sides like it, and the English rate and its history.
quotes: The scutage in England is usually two pounds per knight in 1220.

entries.title: Advice
entries.summary: A vassal's duty to attend his liege's court and give advice, and how a lord uses summonses to control vassals, build consensus, expose rebels and weigh competing interests.
quotes: A vassal asked to attend his liege's court has a duty to attend.

entries.title: Wardship of Heirs
entries.summary: How a liege takes wardship of a dead vassal's heirs and heiresses: fostering, control of the revenues, choice of marriage partners, disparagement, and the value of heirs and heiresses as rewards.
quotes: going straight into the treasury of the liege until the child turns 21 if male, or marries if female

entries.title: Wardship of Widows
entries.summary: How a widow may become the ward of her husband's lord, what portion of the estate she is entitled to, and how the Church views the trade in marriages.
quotes: A widow is entitled to a portion of her husband's estate, fixed at the time of marriage, to maintain herself until her death.

entries.title: Affinity
entries.summary: Defines a magnate's affinity and country as a political bloc, and says players can model it either as a Leadership bonus or by designing key members as agents.
quotes: Players may model the power their character has through affinity in two ways.

entries.title: Church Allies
entries.summary: What a powerful churchman brings as an ally, including military aid from Church manors, the effects and limits of excommunication and interdiction, and lending his Reputation to a cause.
quotes: A powerful churchman can lend his Reputation to a character's cause, so that disinterested or uninformed parties follow his guidance.

entries.title: Affinity Leadership
entries.summary: A bonus from a noble's Affinity score to social Ability rolls dealing with nobles, land-holding ecclesiastics and senior town councilors in his region, graded by rank and reduced when the area is split or the lord neglects his affinity. Examples of rolls it applies to are listed.
quotes: A character may use his Affinity score as a bonus to social Ability rolls that are directly related to his role as a powerful and respected person within a specific region.
The bonus above is halved (round down) if the area is divided between two warring affinities.
+5 For being the senior noble beneath the king in the region (count, earl, duke).

related.text: Chapter Three: A Comparison of Titles

entries.title: Using Intrigue to Aggregate Class Opinion
entries.summary: A stress roll with Intelligence + Intrigue lets a character gauge how an organization or the nobles of a region will react to an event, provided he knows the ruling class there.
quotes: A character may roll a stress die + Intelligence + Intrigue to feel the political mood of an organization, or the nobles of a region.

entries.title: How Small is the Ruling Class of a Kingdom?
entries.summary: Counts of baronies, greater barons and knight's fees in England, showing how small and interrelated the ruling class is, with a note on squires who avoid knighthood for tax reasons.
quotes: These 45 men are all closely related to each other by blood and marriage.

entries.title: The German System
entries.summary: Explains the three sources of German titles (imperial, allodial and local) and their relative status, used to compare German ranks with the French system.
quotes: Assume that an imperial knight has higher status than a free knight, who has higher status than a common knight.

entries.title: Iberian Systems
entries.summary: How Iberian town charters (fueros) shape military service, with a simplified model in which every householder serves unless exempted, fighting either on foot as peons or on horse as caballeros.
quotes: As a simplified version of this model, all people who own a house are expected to serve, unless they have an exemption due to a clause in the fuero.

entries.title: Squire
entries.requires: Gentleman, Knight or Landed Noble Virtue
entries.summary: Describes the squire as a young knight-in-training or as a landholder who has chosen not to take knighthood, and says which social Virtues such a character may take.
quotes: A squire may take the Gentleman, Knight, or Landed Noble Virtues.

entries.title: Bacheler Knight
entries.summary: The household knights of a lord's mesnie: which Virtues and Flaw they normally have, what their lord provides, and how rich bachelers can be Landed Nobles.
quotes: A bacheler knight has the Virtues Knight and Protection, and the Oath of Fealty Flaw or Free Choice.

entries.title: Knight Banneret
entries.summary: The rank of a knight who leads other knights under his own banner, how it is claimed or awarded, and the land and Virtues that go with it, which make it economically close to a Wealthy Landed Noble.
quotes: A knight may claim this rank simply by arriving at a battle with a force of ten knights all clad in his livery and willing to kill as instructed.
Bannerets are always Knights and are generally Landed Nobles.

entries.title: Oath of Fealty (Major Story Flaw)
entries.summary: Optional guidance on adapting the Oath of Fealty Flaw: allodial holders need not have one, and troupes may allow insignificant oaths that do not count as Flaws so knights can still take other Story Flaws.
quotes: A holder of allodial land need not have an Oath of Fealty.

entries.title: Knightly Demands (Major Story Flaw)
entries.requires: Optional rule replacing Oath of Fealty
entries.summary: A variant Major Story Flaw that lets the Storyguide pull any knight into plots typical of medieval ballads, suited to high fantasy, mobile sagas; it replaces Oath of Fealty entirely.
quotes: troupes may simply state that all knights have a Major Story Flaw, called Knightly Demands

entries.title: Landed Noble (Major Virtue)
entries.summary: Extended description of what the Landed Noble Virtue provides at Poor, standard and Wealthy levels: manors, knight service, levies, free seasons per year and spending money.
quotes: He has one season of free time per year.
This Virtue leaves the lord two seasons of free time per year, and ten pounds to spend on largesse, war, or other discretionary matters.
These lands provide the lord with the service of four knights, other than himself, 5 serjants, and 50 villeins.

entries.title: Great Noble (Two Major Virtues)
entries.summary: How the Great Noble Virtue is priced for characters of greater baron rank or higher, and a warning about integrating such characters into a covenant-focused saga.
quotes: Two Major Virtues for characters played in lieu of magi, as major protagonists in the plot.

entries.title: Baron
entries.requires: Virtue: Great Noble or Landed Noble
entries.summary: What it means to be a baron, the difference between greater and lesser barons, the Virtues and Flaw they usually take, military service owed and how much surplus money poor, average and Wealthy barons have.
quotes: A man is considered greater baron if he has at least some land held directly from the king and expenses of at least 400 pounds per year.
An average baron has a surplus of 40 pounds per year that may be spent as he wishes.

entries.title: Earl or Count
entries.summary: The resources of a count or earl: his Virtue, yearly expenditure, the force he is expected to bring to battle, and spending money for average and wealthy counts.
quotes: A count has a yearly expenditure of at least 1000 pounds.
The average count might be required to bring 50 knights to battle, along with their sergeants and 500 infantry.

entries.title: Count Palatine and Marcher Lord
entries.summary: Counts given extra powers on a difficult border, with the special rights of marcher lords and the note that they are effectively Wealthy counts with fewer knights and more infantry.
quotes: Some marcher lords are effectively Wealthy counts.

entries.title: Duke
entries.summary: The standing of a duke or duchess, the Virtue they take and a rough estimate of a duke's personal forces and spending.
quotes: As a rough estimate, a duke has, at minimum, personal forces that include 75 knights, their sergeants, and 750 infantry.

entries.title: King
entries.summary: Defines kingship and succession, and in sidebars gives the scale of a king's lands, income, household army and greater barons, how few families make up the ruling class, and the effects of anointing, including minor magic resistance.
quotes: A king is technically a Great Noble and need not be a Knight, although virtually all are.
All kings have minor magic resistance as noted in Chapter Four: Interference.

related.text: Magic Resistance For Church Officers and Sovereigns

entries.title: How Powerful is a King?
entries.summary: Scale figures for a strong king (demesne share, income, household knights, greater baron vassals and their service) using the King of England as the example.
quotes: A king is technically a Great Noble and need not be a Knight, although virtually all are.

entries.title: Caballero
entries.summary: The requirements and legal protection of a caballero's rank in Iberia, and how to build one as a player character using the Knight Virtue or covenant gear, with local custom usable as a Major Story Flaw.
quotes: Players designing caballeros can either take the Knight Minor Social Status Virtue, or just use gear that belongs to the covenant.

entries.title: Caballero Villano
entries.requires: Wealthy Knight tied to a town
entries.summary: A town-bound mounted warrior who keeps tax exemptions by residing in town and mustering for its defense; tied by his Dependents rather than honor, though troupes may allow Knightly Duties instead.
quotes: This style of Wealthy Knight is tied to the town by his Dependents rather than his honor, although troupes may permit players to select Knightly Duties instead.

entries.title: Caballero Hidalgo (or Fidalgo)
entries.requires: Virtue: Knight and Gentleman or Landed Noble
entries.summary: An ancestral caballero from a family that supports him in matters of honor, comparable to an English lord of the manor, with the Virtues he normally has.
quotes: Hidalgos have the Knight Virtue and either Gentleman or Landed Noble.

entries.title: Ricohombre
entries.summary: The Iberian aristocratic upper class: how their honores work, the military service and restrictions they have, and the Great Noble Virtue they take.
quotes: They have the Great Noble Virtue.

groups.title: Manors and peasants
groups.intro: The manor, its court and peasants, farming and the agricultural year.

entries.title: The Manor: The Model Fief
entries.summary: Defines the manor as the basic game unit of fief, the land needed to support a knight and household, and lists what a typical manor contains.
quotes: A manor, for the purposes of the game, comprises the amount of land traditionally required to maintain a knight, his family, and his household retainers.

related.text: LoM Chapter Three: A Comparison of Titles

entries.title: How Big is a…?
entries.summary: Reference sizes and incomes for acres, manors, hides, virgates, bovates, cottars, villages, towns and cities, with the typical split of peasant holdings and a Terram magic scale for an acre of earth.
quotes: For the sake of simplicity an acre is considered to be 4,840 square yards.
A landed knight's income from a typical manor is twenty pounds per year
Twenty percent have a full virgate, thirty percent have a bovate, and fifty percent are cottars.

entries.title: Farmland
entries.summary: The six legal statuses a piece of land can have and the main land types on a heavily farmed manor.
quotes: Each piece of land has one of six legal statuses.

entries.title: Story Seed: The Foundation Charm
entries.requires: Storyguide use of foundation charms or witch bottles
entries.summary: Describes foundation charms and witch bottles guarding halls, with default Hermetic-equivalent statistics for a witch bottle when Hedge Magic is not available.
quotes: assume that the bottles can detect the magical power to curse (InVi 10, Penetration 5) as well as the Gift (InVi 15, Penetration 0)

entries.title: Arable
entries.summary: How cropland is used and the average sowing rates and yields of winter and spring grain.
quotes: The average winter grain crop is sown at two bushels an acre, and repays that effort with eight bushels of grain.

entries.title: Pasture
entries.summary: Typical flock sizes, grazing rents and shares of sheep, pigs, goats and cattle on a manor.
quotes: As a general rule, the lord has two-thirds of the sheep of any manor in his demesne flock.

entries.title: The Lord's Portion: The Demesne
entries.summary: What the demesne is, how it is worked by villeins, famuli and paid labor, and why free tenants' land is more productive than the lord's.
quotes: Villeins do about a quarter of the work required to plow, sow, and reap the demesne.

entries.title: Waste
entries.summary: Describes the uncultivated waste of a manor as faerie domain outside the blessed fields, with clearing land spreading the Dominion.
quotes: The wasteland is the domain of the faeries.

entries.title: Warrens
entries.summary: The lord's right of warren over small game, covering poaching and even magical creatures that could be familiars or vis sources.
quotes: Magical monsters, including potential familiars and vis sources, may also belong to the lord under the right of warren.

entries.title: Mineral Rights
entries.summary: Who owns minerals found on or beneath land: the king reserves major rights and the lord may charge for any underground resource.
quotes: In Mythic Europe a character who finds a gold nugget, or even a gold mine, doesn't own it

entries.title: Heriot, Mortuary, and Laity Objects
entries.summary: The death duties owed by a peasant to the lord (heriot) and Church (mortuary, laity objects), and their effect on widows.
quotes: The heriot is a death duty owed when the head of a household dies.
Mortuary is technically a fine, not a tax

entries.title: Tallage
entries.summary: The lord's right to demand an arbitrary sum from villeins in proportion to their holdings, its limits in practice, and its commutation to a fixed fee.
quotes: Lords have a right called tallage, which they exercise sparingly, but may legally employ whenever they wish.

entries.title: Trade
entries.summary: How this book treats non-agricultural income: as part of agricultural income or a simple bonus to it, with characters who trade seriously using the City & Guild rules.
quotes: non-agricultural sources of wealth are treated either as an unremarked component of agricultural income or as a bonus to the character's agricultural income.

entries.title: The Manor Court
entries.summary: The three spheres of medieval justice (Church, royal and manorial courts) and which kinds of case the manorial court handles.
quotes: The manorial courts deal with lesser matters.

entries.title: Juries
entries.summary: How manorial juries are empaneled and the three jobs they perform: swearing duties are done, deciding custom, and investigating a matter for the next session.
quotes: A jury may serve three purposes, described below.
Juries of inquisition are groups of men appointed by the court to investigate a matter and report their findings at the next session.

entries.title: Disputes
entries.summary: How disputes between serfs, or between serf and lord, reach the court, which fines they generate for the lord, and the cost of a binding ruling.
quotes: A smaller fine is paid when a dispute is settled amicably outside the court.
the villein pays about a shilling for the court's time and trouble, or two shillings if the case went against him.

entries.title: Disputes Based on Weights and Measures
entries.summary: Explains that there are no standard measures and how natural measures, which tend to favor the lord, are used to settle what is owed.
quotes: There are no standard measures in any kingdom of Mythic Europe.

entries.title: Seizure
entries.summary: A felon's goods pass to his lord, and a new tenant pays a fee to take up vacated land.
quotes: The goods of a felon automatically become the possession of his lord.

entries.title: Sex Taxes: Merchet, Leywrite, Childwrite, and Fines for Celibacy
entries.summary: The fines a lord levies on serfs over marriage, unmarried sex and pregnancy, and celibacy, and who inherits the property of serfs who die childless.
quotes: To secure the permission of the lord, each serf pays a fine called merchet.
Leywrite, the right for laying down, is theoretically an adultery tax.

entries.title: Fines for Being Fined
entries.summary: A peasant fined outside the manorial court owes his lord equivalent compensation, because what he pays is held to belong to the lord.
quotes: The lord owns everything that the peasant owns.

entries.title: Church
entries.summary: The role of the local priest on a manor: curates versus rectors, their duties, who pays them, and the common limits of their education.
quotes: Each is required to preach four sermons a year, although this rule is only weakly enforced.

entries.title: Improvement
entries.summary: When non-magical lords invest in improving their lands, depending on how secure their holdings are.

entries.title: Assarting
entries.summary: Clearing fertile waste into cropland or meadow, how fast a laborer can do it, and how magic can assart land and alarm neighboring lords.
quotes: A single strong laborer with proper tools clears one acre of lightly wooded land per month, if he does no other work.

entries.title: Land Management
entries.summary: Assumes manors have a competent bailiff, so characters cannot improve land just by managing it better unless it was noted as badly run, and says customary businesses are already counted in manor income.
quotes: It is assumed in this section that characters cannot improve their lands simply by managing them better

entries.title: Purchase
entries.summary: Buying land from neighbors costs a multiple of its annual income, adjustable if the seller keeps rights or the buyer takes on dues, and cheaper if paid in immediate coin.
quotes: Characters may purchase land from their neighbors.
Characters can get a better price by paying in immediate coin

entries.title: Discuss Poverty in Your Saga
entries.summary: Optional guidance for the troupe on how realistic the saga's treatment of peasant hardship, noble villainy and Church oppression should be, including simply choosing a covenant's peasants to be happy at creation.
quotes: Troupes should discuss this and choose a degree of realism that suits the stories they wish to tell.

entries.title: Serf or Villein
entries.summary: Legal status of serfs and what they owe their lord in rent, week works and boon works, the censum to buy off week work, and how tradesmen differ from other villeins.
quotes: Serfs owe their lord rent, week works, and boon works.
Rent is traditionally a penny an acre a year, but may be far higher.

entries.title: The Unemployed and Day Workers
entries.summary: The jobless and day-laboring poor outside the planting and reaping seasons, and the rule in some regions that a stranger who stays on a manor long enough becomes the lord's villein.
quotes: the unemployment rate is around twenty percent outside of the planting and reaping seasons.
In France, any stranger who dwells in a manor for more than a year is automatically the villein of the lord

entries.title: Famuli and Other Retained Servants
entries.summary: The lord's retained household servants, how they are housed and fed, and how their status compares with villeins who farm their own land.
quotes: The famuli are the household staff of the lord.

entries.title: Offices for Villeins
entries.summary: How the reeve, beadle, hayward and other village offices are filled, what each does, how they are paid, and why reeves are disliked and corrupt.
quotes: Reeves are usually paid a small wage: generally double whatever is being paid to other laborers
This fee is as high as a shilling a head a year in some places.

entries.title: Free Peasants
entries.summary: What freedom means for a peasant, the service free men may still owe, how freedom passes by birth and marriage, and where free peasants are most common.
quotes: Free peasants make up less than ten percent of the population of most manors

entries.title: Officers
entries.summary: The steward and the bailiff who run a manor for the lord, their duties, accounting obligations, and typical pay by size of holding.
quotes: The steward, or seneschal, is the lord's representative on the manor.
A bailiff is paid approximately ten shillings a year in the smallest fiefs

entries.title: Peasant Loyalty
entries.summary: Peasants are not loyal to strangers, lowering taxes does not simply buy loyalty, and the loyalty of a noble's military household may be tracked with the Covenants loyalty system.
quotes: Peasants in Mythic Europe are not required to be loyal to their lord.
The loyalty of the mesnie may be tracked using the system given in Covenants, page 38

entries.title: Community Loyalty
entries.summary: Magi can keep rich peasants from becoming restive by offering a better deal than a royal charter gives, earning loyalty to the community rather than to the magi themselves.
quotes: Magi can prevent their rich peasants from becoming restive by offering them a deal better than that provided by the nearest town's royal charter.

entries.title: Flight and Rebellion
entries.summary: Explains why the Covenants loyalty mechanic fits large households but not noble-peasant relations, and what drives peasants to flee, rebel, or collectively refuse to work.
quotes: The loyalty mechanic given in Covenants, beginning on page 36
A peasant flees the land when it seems he has better prospects elsewhere.

entries.title: Nothing Grows for the Wicked
entries.requires: Optional folkloric rule chosen by the troupe
entries.summary: An optional folkloric approach in which virtuous, successful characters are blessed with good harvests and community loyalty, replacing the annual harvest roll.
quotes: Troupes using this system select good harvests rather than making the annual roll called for by the Mythic Pound system (see Covenants).

entries.title: Paying Tithes Inadequately
entries.summary: What is owed in tithes, the common ways peasants shortchange the Church, exemptions for the very poor, and how strictly tithes are enforced.
quotes: One tenth of everything that a person gets must be given to the Church.

entries.title: Improvement in Living Standards
entries.summary: Introduces the sinful ways peasants increase their wealth, which make a character richer than pious neighbors.
quotes: Characters performing any of these sins will be substantially wealthier than their more pious neighbors

entries.title: The Economics of Tithing
entries.summary: How heavy tithing is for a peasant and the traditional four-way division of tithes among rector, curate, church fabric and the poor.
quotes: Tithing effectively swallows twenty percent of the income of most peasants.
One-quarter of all tithes go to the rector of the manor.

entries.title: Manumission by Lay Lords
entries.requires: Serf character or covenfolk seeking freedom
entries.summary: How a lay lord frees a serf, what influences the price, and rule-of-thumb costs for a player character to buy freedom or to enter schooling for the priesthood.
quotes: As a rule of thumb, a player character can purchase freedom, for himself and his descendants, for between six and ten pounds.
For player characters, assume this sum to be ten shillings

entries.title: Manumission by Membership of a Town's Guild
entries.summary: A villein becomes free through town guild membership, not just by living in a town for a year and a day; this usually needs a wealthy patron.
quotes: To become free the person must not stray from the town, and must be accepted as a resident by the authorities of the town.

entries.title: The Agricultural Year
entries.summary: How the agricultural year is divided into four uneven seasons by the work done, with the dates each begins and ends.
quotes: The agricultural year is divided into four uneven seasons by the work done at that time, which is dependent on climate.

entries.title: Two or Three Field Rotation
entries.summary: How crops are rotated through fields under the two-field and three-field systems, and how the manor court decides what is planted in each furlong.
quotes: In a three-field manor, wheat or rye is planted in autumn in the first field.

entries.title: May
entries.summary: May labors and festivals, including May Day fires that protect stock against hedge witch curses and Beltaine rituals that can hex magi who have let their Parma Magica lapse outside their Aegis.
quotes: Many peasants run their cattle or sheep between two May Day fires, to defend them against the curses of hedge witches
The Beltaine rituals can hex those who practice magic

entries.title: June
entries.summary: June duties including shearing and plowing, Midsummer beliefs, and how quickly a laborer can cut hay, with the fire risk from damp stacked hay.
quotes: Each laborer can cut about an acre a day in good weather.

groups.title: Towns and guilds
groups.intro: Towns and their charters, guilds and their members, crime and city life.

entries.title: Becoming a Townsman (Citizenship and Sympathetic Connection)
entries.summary: Explains what it takes for a character to become a burgess of a chartered town, and that citizenship creates a sympathetic connection with everyone living under the same charter that can be used to aid magical attacks.
quotes: provide a +1 multiplier bonus to the Penetration score of a magical attack
live in the town continuously for a year and a day

entries.title: Ecclesiastical Lords and Town Divine Aura
entries.summary: Describes how bishops and abbots grant charters and gives the Divine aura level of a town under an ecclesiastical charter, noting that ecclesiastics usually cannot become citizens.
quotes: Towns with ecclesiastical charters have a Divine aura of 3 within the town-walls

related.text: Realms of Power: The Divine p.10

entries.title: Supernatural Charter Lords (Faerie and Demonic Charters)
entries.summary: Covers towns chartered by faerie lords or by demons: the effect on the town's Divine aura, and the typical Infernal Might and services a charter demon offers townsfolk, with their modifiers.
quotes: have a reduced Divine aura of 1 within the townwalls
A typical charter demon has an Infernal Might of 15 (Mentem)
Relief from disease: +2 Living Condition Modifier.

entries.title: Town Occupations Table
entries.summary: A table giving the share of a town's population working in agriculture, craft, service and trade by town size.

entries.title: Minor Covenant Boon: Chartered Town
entries.summary: A covenant boon for a covenant that is itself a chartered town, freeing it from feudal interference and taxes while burdening it with townsfolk who expect to exercise their charter rights.
quotes: This boon is incompatible with the Urban Hook (ArM5, page 74), and cannot be Unknown.

entries.title: Major Covenant Hook: Charter Lord
entries.requires: Covenant creation: Major Hook; covenant must be a large land owner
entries.summary: A covenant hook for a covenant that has granted charters to towns on its lands, drawing the attention of neighbouring lords and the Quaesitores and risking petitions or revolts from its townsfolk.
quotes: This hook may only be taken by a covenant that is a large land owner

entries.title: Town Officials as a Virtue
entries.requires: Optional rule: Town Magistrate Social Status Virtue
entries.summary: Advises treating town office as part of a story, but offers a variant of the Town Magistrate Virtue for a general town official, with the Civil and Canon Law requirement and Academic Abilities benefit dropped.
quotes: a Virtue modeled upon the Minor Social Status Virtue: Town Magistrate (see Crime) can be used

entries.title: Town Defenses and Relic Processions
entries.summary: Describes town walls and gates, and notes that a procession of saints' relics around a threatened town counts as ceremonial influence on a Divine aura.
quotes: This counts as ceremonial influence tempering the aura to Loyal, Calm, or Brave

related.text: Realms of Power: The Divine pp.38-40

entries.title: Craftsman's Stamp (Arcane Connection and Forgery)
entries.summary: A craftsman's stamp on his goods acts as an Arcane Connection to him for a duration depending on how long the item took to make, and the stamp can be forged or altered by magic or skill.
quotes: A stamped good serves as an Arcane Connection to the crafter
this requires a Finesse roll against an Ease Factor of 18

entries.title: Craft Guilds
entries.summary: Describes how craft guilds are organised around a Craft Ability, which towns have them, which appear first, and how guilds split into narrower specialisations in later periods.
quotes: For sagas starting in 1220, guilds generally correspond directly to a particular Craft Ability

entries.title: Number of Guilds in a Town
entries.summary: A rough table of how many guilds a town has by population size and by saga date.
quotes: 1,000 or less | 0–1

entries.title: Guild Member Ages and Abilities
entries.summary: A table of suggested ages, Craft scores and secondary Abilities for each guild rank, used as a guideline when creating guild member characters.
quotes: Journeyman | 5 | 2 (Bargain)

entries.title: Abusive Lengths of Apprenticeship
entries.summary: An optional rule giving longer apprenticeships for certain guilds, and how the extra years of experience are earned and applied.
quotes: Instead of the regular seven years of apprenticeship, use the lengths listed on the table below.

entries.title: Guild Members (Ranks, Roster and Required Abilities)
entries.summary: Introduces guild ranks, the guild roster, and the Abilities guild members need, including minimum Guild Lore scores by rank.
quotes: Journeymen need at least a Guild Lore score of 1, masters need a 2, and senior masters and deans must have a Guild Lore score of 3.

entries.title: Guild Apprentices (Advancement and Apprentice Piece)
entries.requires: Virtue: Guild Apprentice (or Craftsman for non-guild apprentices)
entries.summary: Rules for apprentice characters: the Virtue required, how the seven years of apprenticeship translate into seasons of experience and which Abilities may receive it, and the apprentice piece test that ends the apprenticeship.
quotes: Starting guild apprentice characters must buy the Minor Social Status Virtue Guild Apprentice.
an apprentice character receives two seasons of Exposure experience, one season of Practice experience, and one season of Training a year
The apprentice makes a Primary Characteristic + Craft Ability + stress die roll against an Ease Factor of 9.

entries.title: Journeymen (Requirements, Contracts and Promotion)
entries.summary: Describes journeyman characters: the Virtue, age and Craft requirements, how the wage contract is bargained for, joining a guild in another town via a harder apprentice piece, the cost and vote needed to become a master, and annual dues.
quotes: Journeymen characters must buy the Minor Social Status Virtue Journeyman.
a Communication + Bargain + (Age / 10, rounded up) stress roll against a variable Ease Factor
The Ease Factor for this piece should be increased from 9 to 12.

entries.title: Making a Journeyman Contract
entries.summary: A table converting the result of a journeyman's contract-bargaining roll into a modifier on the Labor Points he earns, with modifiers for his history with the master, his Craft score and past guild fines.
quotes: Communication + Bargain + (Age/10, rounded up) + a stress die
+2 Appropriate Craft Ability is 8+

entries.title: Guild Masters
entries.summary: Requirements for master characters and how many workers a master can employ, with a Labor Point penalty for being understaffed.
quotes: Master characters must have the Minor Social Status Virtue Guild Master.
A master can employ a number of apprentices and journeymen equal to his Leadership score.
Subtract 3 Labor Points for every absent worker from the number of Labor Points the master accrues in a season.

entries.title: Senior Masters
entries.summary: Requirements for senior master characters and how many workshops they can operate.
quotes: Character senior masters may effectively operate a number of workshops equal to one half their Leadership score rounded up.

entries.title: Guild Officials and Inquisitors
entries.requires: Virtue: Senior Master (to play an official)
entries.summary: Describes the board of guild officials, how they are chosen, their terms, powers (including defrocking masters), and the inquisitors who inspect workshops; playing an official needs no extra mechanic beyond the Virtue.
quotes: Guild officials retain their office for six months, at which point they return to the pool of senior master candidates.
Substandard goods are confiscated on the spot, with a fine equal to the goods' value imposed on the master.

entries.title: Guild Dean
entries.summary: How deans are selected and removed, the starting requirements for a dean character, and the stipend a dean receives from his guild.
quotes: he should be at least 50 years of age, have a Craft Ability of at least, 7 and have Bargain, Leadership, and Guild Lore scores of 5 or more
This stipend runs from 20 to 40 pounds, and can include properties like a large house or an additional workshop.

entries.title: Craftswomen and the Male Guild Sponsor
entries.requires: Female guild character (Virtue: Male Guild Sponsor)
entries.summary: Explains how women are restricted in guilds and the ways they enter them through a father's or husband's name on the roster, and how the Male Guild Sponsor Virtue lets a female character join any guild in a saga.
quotes: allows female characters to participate in any guild of the player's choice
Even if a woman gains the status of a master, she is legally forbidden the opportunity to be a guild official.

entries.title: Service Guilds
entries.summary: Service guilds follow the craft guild rules, with Profession replacing Craft for ability requirements and labor pools replacing workshops.
quotes: Replace the requirement for specific scores in a Craft Ability with a requirement for the same score in a Profession Ability.

groups.title: Crafts and workshops
groups.intro: Craftsmen at work: Labor Points, workshops, production and quality.

entries.title: Income Bands (Trivial to Legendary)
entries.summary: Defines the six bands of annual profit (Trivial, Minor, Lesser, Typical, Greater, Legendary), what each means as spending money after expenses, example enterprises, and which Social Status Virtues buy each band.
quotes: The income figure listed below for each band is the amount of money a character in that band could spend frivolously in a year without damaging his source of income.
A single workshop, in an average craft, earns 10 Mythic Pounds for its owner each year.

entries.title: Labor and Livelihood (Labor Points)
entries.summary: Characters who work for a living earn Labor Points each season spent tending their business, multiplied by wealth, and must spend a set number to maintain their enterprise.
quotes: A character gains (primary Characteristic + Craft) or (Communication + Profession) Labor Points per season worked.
It costs 36 Labor Points to maintain a character's business interests at their current level.

entries.title: Improving Wealth and Social Status
entries.summary: Gives the Labor Point costs of moving between Poor, average and Wealthy, what happens when a character loses wealth or status, and the extra season and stories needed to reach higher income bands.
quotes: To move from Poor to average costs 120 points.
To move from average to Wealthy costs 360 points.
Moving to a higher income band costs the Labor Points noted above, but also costs a season of time.

entries.title: Overwork (Reputation Penalties)
entries.summary: Working extra seasons or living below one's means to gain Labor Points faster earns a negative Reputation for impiety or miserliness.
quotes: A character who is not Poor, but works three or more seasons in a year, gains a negative Reputation.
This imposes 1 or 3 experience in a Reputation for miserliness every year.

entries.title: Labor Points from Stories
entries.summary: Stories that improve a character's economic or social status award extra Labor Points, scaled by how central the merchant is to the story.
quotes: Half a season's worth of Labor Points when they are a subplot of a more significant story, dealt with by magi.
Two seasons' worth of Labor Points when the merchant is the central character of the story.

entries.title: Investing Time
entries.summary: Characters can invest Labor Points as time or profits to improve their business, treated as minor stories that are not actually played.
quotes: Characters may invest their time or profits, as represented by Labor Points, to improve their businesses.

entries.title: Money and Investment (Labor Points to Pounds)
entries.summary: Explains that Labor Points cannot be directly converted to money, and gives a guideline table of what a block of Labor Points is worth in pounds for each income band.
quotes: the average character earns around 6 Labor Points a season, multiplied according to his level of wealth
This means that 9 Labor Points are worth:

entries.title: Craftsmen (Regular Craftsman Characters)
entries.summary: Rules for non-guild craftsman characters: the free Virtue, the Abilities they need, how many apprentices they may train, and how rural, urban, monastic and covenant craftsmen differ.
quotes: A regular craftsman character must have the Free Social Virtue Craftsman.
Bargain and Craft are the only two mandatory Abilities that an average, non-guild member craftsman character needs.
A regular craftsman may have a number of apprentices at a single time equal to his Leadership score.

entries.title: Companions vs. Grogs for Craftsmen
entries.summary: Clarifies that companion and grog status depends on narrative role rather than craft rank, while the Virtue and Flaw limits for each type still apply.
quotes: Companions and grogs are defined by their narrative role

entries.title: Laborers (Laborer Characters)
entries.summary: A laborer character has the free Laborer Virtue and a Profession Ability instead of a Craft Ability, with that Profession also covering wage negotiations.
quotes: A laborer character must have the free Social Status Virtue Laborer.

entries.title: Covenant Craftsmen
entries.summary: Options for deciding how covenant craftsmen relate to guilds, from simply treating all of them as regular craftsmen to making them expelled, runaway or illegal guild members, and how trade-based covenants sell their goods.
quotes: The simplest method is to make every craftsman a regular craftsman.

entries.title: Crafting Items (Seasonal Production)
entries.summary: Introduces the seasonal rules for a craftsman's output, in which craftsmen work only part of the year, and says storyguide craftsmen only need these rules when asked to make a specific item.
quotes: For purposes of the total amount of goods produced in a year, storyguide characters are only allowed three seasons of actual work.
Storyguide character craftsmen are assumed to be busily working in their workshops

entries.title: The Craft Ability (Defined by Vocation)
entries.summary: Rules clarification that a Craft Ability is normally named by the character's vocation rather than by the material worked, with a survey of the materials common crafts use.
quotes: a craftsman should define his Craft Abilities by vocation rather than material

entries.title: Working with Related Material
entries.summary: Penalties to a craftsman's Craft score when he works with raw materials outside his usual field, and the loss of his specialization bonus.
quotes: Treat his Craft score as one less for determining his success.
the character's Craft score is penalized by three

entries.title: The Workshop
entries.summary: How long a workshop takes to build, what it costs for inexpensive, standard and expensive goods, and why workshop size does not affect production the way a laboratory's size does.
quotes: Workshops for inexpensive goods cost one Mythic Pound to construct, while those for standard goods cost two, and those for expensive goods cost five.
It takes a season to build such a workshop

entries.title: Craft Specialization
entries.summary: Guidance on choosing a Craft specialization: a single item, workshop activity or quality of goods, giving a bonus to that narrow aspect of the Ability.
quotes: The intent of the specialization rules is to allow a character to gain a +1 bonus to a single aspect of a broader Ability.

entries.title: Workshop Innovation
entries.summary: A workshop has an Innovation score added to its Workshop Total, raised by spending Labor Points and a season of work, with a table of the cumulative Labor Point cost for each level.
quotes: The workshop's Innovation score is added to the Workshop Total.
It takes 100 Labor Points to increase Innovation to +1, 200 more Labor Points for a +2 Innovation score, and another 300 Labor Points to have a +3 Innovation score

entries.title: Raw Materials (Workshop Raw Materials Score)
entries.summary: A workshop has a Raw Materials score improved by spending Labor Points and a season; unlike Innovation it is lost if the responsible character leaves and must be maintained at a Labor Point cost each year.
quotes: It takes 50 Labor Points to increase the Raw Material score to 1, 100 more Labor Points to increase it to 2, and an additional 150 Labor Points to increase the score to 3
It costs 5 Labor Points per point of Raw Material to sustain a business with a positive Raw Material score.

entries.title: Craftsman Workshop Total and Craft Level
entries.summary: Introduces the five quality grades of finished goods and the Workshop Total (primary Characteristic + Craft Ability + the workshop's Innovation and Raw Materials) that a craftsman compares against a Craft Level to see what a season's work produces.
quotes: Workshop Total: Primary Characteristic + Ability + Innovation + Raw Materials
If the Workshop Total equals or exceeds the Craft Level, the character produces a specific amount and quality of finished goods.

entries.title: Primary Characteristic of a Craft
entries.summary: Sidebar saying which Characteristic a craft or labour uses in its formulas (usually Dexterity for craftsmen, Strength for laborers, with exceptions the troupe decides).
quotes: A common rule of thumb is that craftsmen use Dexterity and laborers use Strength.

entries.title: Finished Goods and Quality Craft Levels
entries.summary: Sets the standard Craft Level for a season's work and the Craft Levels needed for shoddy, standard, superior, excellent and wondrous goods; a Workshop Total below standard yields shoddy goods and the storyguide may raise the Craft Level for adverse conditions.
quotes: The standard Craft Level, which assumes adequate space, necessary materials, and no distractions, is 6.
Craft Level for Standard Items: 6
Craft Level for Wondrous Items: 12 + Magnitude of Effect

entries.title: Modifying the Craft Level (situation table)
entries.summary: Sidebar table of situational increases to the Craft Level (war, famine, plague, scarce materials, interruptions, staff changes, non-mundane auras); changing the base Craft Level shifts the levels for every quality grade equally.
quotes: Modifying the basic Craft Level also changes the Craft Levels of different quality goods.
if the storyguide decides that the Basic Craft Level is 9, then a craftsman character needs a 15 to make superior goods and an 18 to make excellent goods.

entries.title: Seasonal Production Chart (scaling output by Craft score)
entries.summary: Explains how to scale the number of items a craftsman makes in a season from his Craft Ability score, and how to convert seasonal output into days per item.
quotes: Divide the character's Craft Ability score by five, then multiply this number by the number of items that a basic craftsman would make in a season.
divide 72 (which is the number of working days in a season, derived from 12 six-day weeks) by the number of items constructed in a season.

entries.title: Standard Quality Items Constructed in a Season (table)
entries.summary: Table of how many standard-quality goods of each kind a craftsman of average skill makes in a season, with the responsible guild and cost band, plus notes on large items that take several seasons and on teams and labor gangs.
quotes: Instead, round to the nearest nice fraction.

entries.title: Shoddy Quality Items
entries.summary: Shoddy goods look and perform like standard goods but break on a botch, and a craftsman can spot them with a Perception roll.
quotes: making a Perception + Craft Ability + simple roll against an Ease Factor of 6

entries.title: Superior Quality Items
entries.summary: Superior goods give a small bonus to one feature (strength, durability or appearance) for a specific activity; only one such bonus applies to any single roll or total, and the entry gives examples for clothing, tools, shields, swords and armor.
quotes: Only one bonus from a superior or excellent quality item applies to a single total or roll, no matter how many such items are used.

entries.title: Crafted Item Quality and Enchanting
entries.summary: Sidebar giving the Lab Total penalty or bonus a magus gets for enchanting an item of shoddy, standard, superior or excellent quality, and noting that wondrous goods count as superior and lose their non-Hermetic effects when enchanted.
quotes: Regular, standard quality goods subtract one from a maga's Lab Total, and shoddy goods subtract three.
If a magus is enchanting a crafted item — be it a boot, blade, or broom — the item must be of at least superior quality.

entries.title: Excellent Quality Items
entries.summary: Excellent goods earn extra bonuses for each block of points the Workshop Total exceeds the Craft Level, limited by the creator's Craft Ability, and the bonus applies to every use of the item.
quotes: For every 3 points that exceed the Craft Level, add an additional +1 bonus to a feature of the item.
Total Bonus Limit: Craft Ability / 3, rounded up

entries.title: Workshop Assistants
entries.summary: Craftsmen may employ apprentices or journeymen up to a limit set by Leadership, and each assistant boosts the Workshop Total by a fraction of his own Craft Ability.
quotes: Each assistant adds half his Craft Ability score to the Workshop Total.

entries.title: Craftsman Manuals
entries.summary: A literate craftsman can spend a Labor Point and a season to write a manual of his process; other craftsmen doing that activity may add its score to their Workshop Total, with only one manual usable per season.
quotes: he produces a manual that has a score of one-third his Craft Ability score, rounded up
A craft manual adds its score to the Workshop Total.

entries.title: Workshop Exertion
entries.summary: A craftsman may push his workshop to boost the Workshop Total with a simple die, at the cost of an Aging roll each season and a roll on the Workshop Exertion Results table.
quotes: When a character exerts himself in the workshop, add a simple die roll to the Workshop Total.
For every season that a character exerts himself, the player must make an Aging roll, regardless of the craftsman's actual age.

entries.title: Workshop Exertion Results (table)
entries.summary: Sidebar table and descriptions for the stress-die outcome of exerting in the workshop, from disaster through story events, inventions, increased Reputation and increased understanding.
quotes: Put a simple die's worth of Labor Points towards the workshop's Innovation score.
Add a simple die worth of experience points to the craftsman's (Craft) Reputation score.

entries.title: Craftsman Reputations
entries.summary: Each craftsman has a (Craft) Reputation that rises with excellent seasons and wondrous items and falls with repeated shoddy work.
quotes: Any season a craftsman has a Workshop Total 6 or more points over the necessary Craft Level to produce standard quality goods, the character earns 1 experience point.

entries.title: Selling Finished Goods
entries.summary: A craftsman may roll to haggle a better price, either against a fixed Ease Factor or in opposition to an important customer, with the price moving in fixed percentage steps up to a maximum.
quotes: Presence + Bargain + simple die vs. Ease Factor 9
If successful, the character sells the item for 10% above its standard cost.

entries.title: Basic Laborer's Service
entries.summary: Laborers use a Labor Total compared against a Profession Level in the same way craftsmen use Workshop Totals, producing shoddy, standard or superior service but never excellent or wondrous.
quotes: Labor Level is the laboring character's primary Characteristic + Profession Ability and the Profession Level has a base of 6

entries.title: Wondrous Items (craftsman-made minor enchantments)
entries.summary: How a craftsman with Touched by (Realm) makes a non-Hermetic wondrous item for a specific customer: limits on its single effect, its Craft Level built from a base plus the magnitude and daily uses, how Workshop Total progress accumulates over seasons, helper limits, Arcane Connection to the recipient and verbal triggers.
quotes: Base Supernatural Item Craft Level: 12 + Magnitude of Hermetic Effect + Modifier for Number of Uses per Day
To create wondrous items, a character must have the Major Supernatural Virtue Touched by (Realm).
Wondrous items have no Penetration scores and cannot affect anyone with even the slightest Magic Resistance.

related.text: ArM5 p.110 Shape and Material Bonus chart

entries.title: Craftsmen Supernatural Virtues (Eye of Hephaestus, Touched by (Realm), Crafter's Healing)
entries.requires: Virtue: Eye of Hephaestus, Touched by (Realm) or Crafter's Healing
entries.summary: Sidebar describing three craftsman-only Supernatural Virtues and the rolls they use: judging an item's quality and magic, enabling wondrous items, and the Crafter's Healing Ability for healing wounds at a cost in fatigue and Warping.
quotes: make a Perception + Awareness + stress die roll against an Ease Factor of 9
Make a Presence + Crafter's Healing + stress die roll against an Ease Factor equal to the Improvement Ease Factor determined by the Wound Recovery Table (ArM5, page 179).

entries.title: Damaged Goods: Stress Checks and Damage Levels
entries.summary: When a story event or a botch threatens a valued item, its owner makes a stress check; failures remove damage levels, which depend on the item's quality and Size, until the item breaks. Covers modifiers, botches, unnatural use, and the different fate of wondrous and Hermetic items.
quotes: Stress Check: stress die + modifiers vs. Ease Factor 15
If the stress check fails, the item loses one of its damage levels.
Wondrous items made by craftsmen cease to function if they sustain any damage.

related.text: Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults (House Verditius repairs)

entries.title: Locks and Keys (making, breaking, picking)
entries.summary: Sidebar on crafting locks (a high base Craft Level boosted by Artes Liberales), their doubled damage levels, and the rolls for breaking, pulling apart or picking a lock at different qualities.
quotes: Locks are very hard to make, and the base Craft Level is 15, which is subject to the same modifications as other Craft Levels.
Make a Dexterity + Legerdemain + stress die roll against an Ease Factor of 12 to open a standard quality lock.

entries.title: Repairing Damaged Goods
entries.summary: A craftsman who could make an item can repair it without a roll over a season, paying Labor Points per damage level, but broken items cannot be repaired.
quotes: He must also spend one Labor Point for every damage level he repairs.

groups.title: Trade, money and wealth
groups.intro: Money, prices, merchants, fairs and trade.

entries.title: Negotiation (Bargain rolls)
entries.summary: Procedure for haggling over a price: appraise the goods' value, make opposed Bargain rolls for buyer and seller, derive the lowest final price from the difference, and optionally roll to read the seller's willingness.
quotes: The buyer can attempt to determine the value by making a Perception + Bargain roll, with an Ease Factor of 9.
Communication + Bargain + simple die for the buyer and seller
Regardless of how good the buyer's Bargain roll is, the sale price is never less than half of the initial value.

entries.title: Weights and Measures (unit conversions)
entries.summary: Sidebar of conversion tables for length, capacity, weight, and the separate scales used for gold and silver and for apothecaries, as a guide to retail units.
quotes: 4 quarts = 1 gallon
16 ounces = 1 pound

entries.title: Grant of a Fair
entries.summary: Who may be granted a fair, the profit and running cost of a medium fair, and how owning a fair rates as a covenant source of income under the Minor Resources Boon.
quotes: A typical annual fair for a town counts as a Lesser Source of Income
for the Minor Resources Boon Rights

related.text: Covenants p.16 Minor Resources Boon Rights

entries.title: The Champagne Cycle (fair calendar and trading order)
entries.summary: Sidebar giving the dates and durations of the Champagne fairs and how trade in each six-week fair is regulated into set-up, cloth, leather, other goods and settling of accounts.
quotes: Generally there is an interval of about two weeks in between fairs.

entries.title: The English Fair Cycle (fair calendar and owners)
entries.summary: Sidebar listing the major English fairs with their dates and owners.
quotes: Stamford: Ash Wednesday to Palm Sunday (owner: Earl Warenne)

entries.title: Hermetic Mid-Summer Fair
entries.summary: A gathering hosted by a Greater Alps covenant where magi trade vis, books and enchanted devices, with individual deals or an auction run by the Quaesitores, using barter or vis as currency.
quotes: All exchanges are by barter or by use of vis as currency.

entries.title: Virtues and Flaws for Traders (Social Status choices)
entries.summary: Every trader takes a Social Status Virtue matching the style of trade, in order of wealth: Merchant, Merchant Adventurer, Factor and Capo, adjusted by Wealthy or Poor; lists other Virtues and Flaws that suit merchant characters.
quotes: All traders have a Social Status Virtue representing the style of trade in which they engage.
These Virtues, in ascending order of wealth, are: Merchant (which suits urban merchants and local carriers), Merchant Adventurer, Factor, and Capo.

entries.title: Trading Companies (capo, partners, factors)
entries.summary: How a trading company is structured around a capo, partners and distant factors, how traders may work for a company, and how Employed by a Company interacts with Poor and Wealthy.
quotes: A character may have both the Employed by a Company and Poor Flaws, but this requires an explanation approved by the troupe

entries.title: Trade and the Order of Hermes
entries.summary: Warns that Hermetic magic gives traders huge advantages and points troupes at the Inflation rules in Covenants when generating vast wealth.
quotes: should familiarize themselves with the Inflation rules given in Covenants, Chapter 5: Wealth & Poverty

entries.title: Creating Wealth Using Magic
entries.summary: List of ways magi can generate profit with magic, from gathering and manufacturing goods to shrinking cargo, magical crews and faster travel.
quotes: Magi are able to create wealth almost effortlessly.

entries.title: Novelties (optional technologies for trade)
entries.summary: Optional innovations (business correspondence, deposit banking, insurance, letters of exchange, rudders, saws, vertical integration and others) that magi could introduce to change trade in a saga.
quotes: Most cranes can handle only about two and a half tons of carefully stowed cargo

entries.title: The Urban Merchant
entries.summary: Describes the urban merchant, the least affluent trader type, who retails in one city, and what such a character offers a covenant.
quotes: They should select the Merchant Social Status Virtue.

entries.title: Urban Merchant Scale of Affluence
entries.summary: Describes poor, average and wealthy urban merchants by lifestyle, home and trade.
quotes: Wealthy merchants own their own home, and trade from a store near the market that they might own.

entries.title: Investments Suited to All Merchants
entries.summary: Introduces the ways any merchant can invest surplus Labor Points or spare seasons.
quotes: All merchant types may invest their surplus Labor Points, or spend their spare seasons, in the following ways.

entries.title: Charity (investing Labor Points)
entries.summary: Giving surplus labor to charity improves Reputation, gives social contacts, and lets the merchant summon a crowd of the people the charity helps, sized by a formula using Communication, Leadership, Reputation and a Social Status Multiplier.
quotes: a number of people respond equal to the character's (Communication + Leadership) x his Reputation resulting from charity work x a Social Status Multiplier.

entries.title: Commodity Speculation (investing Labor Points)
entries.summary: Storing goods in hope of a price rise returns Labor Points each year on the amount invested, requires storage and guards, and can be lost to story events.
quotes: The return for commodity speculation is 1 Labor Point per year for every 10 invested

entries.title: Drawings (trading Labor Points for fine goods)
entries.summary: Merchants can spend Labor Points on sumptuous hand-sized goods, and an introduction-agent activity returns part of the invested Labor Points in exchange for a Favor.
quotes: Every (1 x Wealth Multiplier) Labor Points spent is worth a single sumptuous item of hand tool size or smaller.

entries.title: Marriage Broker (investing seasons)
entries.summary: Spending seasons of Labor Points to arrange a marriage earns Reputation, temporary Social Contacts and Favors owed by the couple or their parents.
quotes: This costs two seasons' worth of Labor Points, which are lost.

entries.title: Market Changes (booms, crop failure, new products)
entries.summary: Story and investment rules for booms (an Intelligence + Area Lore roll with graded outcomes when investing), crop failures and famine, and new products, with the Labor Point gains each can earn.
quotes: a character can detect a boom coming by making an Intelligence + Area Lore roll
A roll of 18 lets a character prepare for years in advance
A product that spawns its own industries provides four seasons worth of Labor Points

entries.title: Legal Action (investment of time)
entries.summary: Besides the story, a merchant may bring a lawsuit as an investment of time, resolved by opposed Intelligence + Law rolls with modifiers for true or false claims and a change to a Reputation on a win.
quotes: The merchant compares the Intelligence + Civil or Canon Law roll of his representative with that of his opponent

entries.title: The Local Carrier
entries.summary: Describes local carriers, who work one route with stable goods, the waterman variant, and how they serve covenants.
quotes: All local traders have the Merchant Virtue.

entries.title: Local Carrier Scale of Abundance
entries.summary: Describes the cargo, home and staff of poor, average and wealthy local carriers.
quotes: A local carrier of average wealth carries enough cargo to fill a single four-wheeled cart.

entries.title: Smuggling (setting up and investing time)
entries.summary: Smuggling as a story reward and as an investment of time that yields Labor Points from Intelligence and Intrigue, with the Flaw and Virtue that smugglers acquire.
quotes: Smuggling, as an investment of time, earns (Intelligence + Intrigue) x Wealth Multiplier Labor Points per season.

entries.title: The Merchant Adventurer
entries.summary: Describes the merchant adventurer who commands a ship or caravan, how the crew is built from the travel chapter's notes, and the city's expectations in time of war.
quotes: All merchant adventurers, regardless of wealth or poverty, are in command of a ship, or a caravan of wagons or pack beasts.

entries.title: Ventures (planning a trading voyage)
entries.summary: Factors a merchant weighs when planning a venture with no certain buyer: return cargo, languages of trade, bulk versus luxury goods, and crew size traded against cargo space.
quotes: Extra crew take up cargo space at the rate of one ton per eight additional sailors.

related.text: City & Guild Chapter 5: Travel, Ship Combat

entries.title: Convoys and Caravans
entries.summary: Leading a convoy earns Reputation and Labor Points as a story or as an investment of time, and a failed convoy damages Reputation.
quotes: half a season's worth of Labor Points per season as an investment of time

entries.title: Finding Investors
entries.summary: A merchant adventurer needs a backer for each venture until his Reputation is high enough, and a season spent winning a sponsor earns Labor Points as a story or investment.
quotes: until the merchant has a positive Reputation of at least 3

entries.title: Warfare and Blockades (blockade running)
entries.summary: How war reroutes trade, and the seasonal shiphandling roll a blockade-runner makes against an Ease Factor to slip past the besiegers.
quotes: Blockade running requires a seasonal shiphandling roll (Dexterity + suitable Profession) against an Ease Factor of 15

entries.title: The Factor
entries.summary: Describes the factor who manages a trading house's assets in one city, his role and the Abilities factors typically have.
quotes: Factors are skilled in Bargain, Civil or Common Law, Folk Ken, Leadership, and Profession Trader.

entries.title: Factor Scale of Affluence
entries.summary: Describes the lifestyle of poor, average and wealthy factors, company versus independent, and the consequences of failing to keep up appearances.
quotes: The Factor Virtue is also used for independent traders who have sufficient capital to organize multiple shipments

entries.title: Change of Government (investment of time)
entries.summary: A factor can win over a new ruler as a story, or as an investment of time that yields Labor Points from Communication and Intrigue and the Favor of a minor political figure.
quotes: (Communication + Intrigue) x Wealth multiplier Labor Points

entries.title: Company Neighborhood (warehouses and guards)
entries.summary: Costs and staffing for a trading house's warehouse and the neighborhood built around it, including guards per ton of cargo and the season a factor spends supervising construction.
quotes: Replacing a warehouse costs 10 pounds per hundred tons of cargo storage space.
most warehouses hire one guard for every ten tons of cargo

entries.title: House Reputation (advocates and largesse)
entries.summary: A merchant house has Reputations that its representatives borrow and change; they can be improved by representatives' deeds, hired advocates (limited to a small modifier) and largesse such as festivals and public buildings, with a cap on advocates per person.
quotes: Several advocates working together can warp a victim's perception of the house markedly, but cannot ever produce a Reputation modifier greater than 3.
No person may be influenced by more than three advocates, altering the same Reputation, at the same time.

entries.title: Skullduggery (hiring criminals with Intrigue)
entries.summary: Characters committing commercial crime through hired professionals roll Communication + Intrigue in place of the proxy's roll when the crime is not played out as a story.
quotes: the hiring character rolls Communication + Intrigue and uses the result in place of the proxy's roll

entries.title: Assassination, Beatings and Kidnapping (costs)
entries.summary: Typical prices for hired assassins, beatings and kidnappings, and the Reputation cost of habitually having poor people attacked.
quotes: An assassin usually charges two pounds for this service.

entries.title: Bribes
entries.summary: Bribe sizes scale with the official's wage and the risk of the favor, from a week's to a year's wages, with recurring favors paid as a percentage.
quotes: An easily granted favor costs a week's wages.

entries.title: Sabotage
entries.summary: Hired agents attempt sabotage with a Dexterity + Stealth roll against the best sentry's Perception + Awareness roll, with a bonus for each extra sentry and for the type of sabotage.
quotes: Sabotage requires a Dexterity + Stealth + stress roll that exceeds the Perception + Awareness + stress roll of the most skilled sentry guarding the facility that the agent seeks to harm.

entries.title: Sabotage Table
entries.summary: Table of the sentry's Awareness bonus by type of sabotage, from defacement to spoilage, with examples.

entries.title: Spying
entries.summary: Factors keep spies, often at little cost, but spies asked to betray their own business demand very large payments.
quotes: Spies require very large payments for their assistance, sometimes as much as they earn by their legitimate profession.

entries.title: Theft
entries.summary: Large-scale theft between rival houses needs at least a brief story, and the thieves usually demand a share of the stolen cargo's value.
quotes: The thieves working for the characters usually request at least half the value of the stolen cargo for their effort, in coin.

entries.title: Largesse: The Costs of Excellent Building (table)
entries.summary: Table of the cost in pounds of public works such as monuments, roads, wells, bridges, mills, chapels and churches that a house may sponsor to improve its Reputation.

entries.title: Young Talent (investment of time)
entries.summary: Recruiting young merchants into the house earns Labor Points as a story, or as an investment of time by rolling Communication + Leadership times the Wealth Multiplier, plus Favors owed by the recruits.
quotes: As an investment of time, roll [{Communication + Leadership} x Wealth Multiplier] and gain that number of Labor Points

entries.title: The Capo
entries.summary: Describes the capo who leads a merchant company, sets its strategy and culture, and what a capo offers a covenant.
quotes: All characters with this role must select the Capo Social Status Virtue.

entries.title: Capo Scale of Affluence
entries.summary: Describes poor, average and wealthy capos and the role of the capo's house as the company's central office.
quotes: An average capo lives luxuriously, like a nobleman.

entries.title: Personal Pleasure and Aggrandizement (entertaining guests)
entries.summary: A capo may throw a lavish themed party as an investment of time, rolling a die plus Characteristic plus the theme Ability with bonus from money spent, and gains Favors from the result; also notes local etiquette on display and marriage.
quotes: A capo may entertain guests as an investment of time, throwing a lavish party, lasting days, that emphasizes a particular Ability.
The character gains the benefits of one Favor Flaw for every five points of this total, rounding up.

entries.title: Commercial Sources of Trade Goods (reading the lists)
entries.summary: Explains how to read the regional lists of trade goods: only major export sources are listed, italics mark famous exporters, and cheap or fine markers say which qualities are available.
quotes: If a commodity is marked as cheap, then only standard and shoddy goods are available at that rate, while commodities marked fine include superior and excellent versions.

entries.title: Prices of Goods
entries.summary: Explains the universal price table for commodities by quality, quoted in Mythic Pounds of silver per tun or ton, so players producing wealth magically can value what they create.
quotes: All prices are in Mythic Pounds of silver per tun or ton.

entries.title: Trade Weights and Measures (ton, tun, pound, yard)
entries.summary: Conversion factors between retail units for dry goods, grain, liquids and cloth and the ton or tun used for bulk prices.
quotes: 16 ounces = 1 pound = 1/2,240 ton
A tun defines the weight of a ton.

entries.title: Prices of Goods Table
entries.summary: Table of commodity prices per ton in Mythic Pounds for shoddy, standard, superior and expensive qualities, with notes on unavailable grades and goods sold by other units.

entries.title: Medieval Money
entries.summary: Explains coins versus moneys-of-account and the fixed relationship between pound, shilling, penny and mark in the West, and how eastern bezants and denars relate to them.
quotes: In the West, a Mythic Pound equals 20 Mythic Shillings and 240 Mythic Pennies.
In the East, a Mythic Pound equals two Mythic Bezants or Denars.

entries.title: Price List (common goods and quality multipliers)
entries.summary: Sample prices for everyday goods for story flavor, extrapolated by the troupe for unlisted items, plus quality multipliers applied to a price from shoddy to wondrous; not intended for working out merchants' or craftsmen's yearly income.
quotes: Adjust the price of an item by its quality.

versions.title: Price list (Covenants)
versions.summary: Rough price tables in Mythic Pounds for animals, books, buildings, Hermetic items, hospitality, labor, land, precious materials, travel, and weapons and armor.
quotes: prices are quoted in whole Mythic Pounds

entries.title: Quality and Size Multipliers
entries.summary: Multipliers applied to price list costs for item quality and size, which stack when both apply.
quotes: | Excellent / Huge | x 5 |
something that is both Huge and of Excellent quality has a total multiplier of 25.

entries.title: Knights' wealth: the simple system
entries.summary: Recaps the core wealth system in which wealth is relative to social class and set by Social Status and Virtues and Flaws, and how fiefs gain value as story rewards.
quotes: a character's level of wealth is an effect of social status, modified by Virtues and Flaws like Wealthy or Poor

entries.title: Knights' wealth in Mythic Pounds
entries.summary: Recaps the Mythic Pound accounting system and applies it to a knight's manor, breaking down his expenses, surplus and income, and the cost of knight service.
quotes: Each Mythic Pound can be divided into 20 shillings or 240 pence.
assume that a knight makes ten pounds each year for each manor that does not owe knight service.

entries.title: Merchants and Bankers (Vis Exchange, Loans, Liens, Pawning)
entries.summary: How Redcaps trade vis between Technique and Form types at fixed exchange rates, and lend, pawn, take liens and speculate on vis and magic items, including interest rates, loan limits, vis accounts, notary letters and Tribunal treasuries.
quotes: Generally, they trade one unit of vis for two.
Fair practice is to both pay and charge 20% interest annually
ten pounds of silver might be considered roughly equivalent to a pawn of vis

entries.title: Vis Notation
entries.summary: Explains the abbreviations used in vis accounting: pigni (pawns), and the occasional larger units of rooks and queens.
quotes: ten of these pawns made a "rook," and ten rooks made a "queen."

entries.title: Usurers (High-Interest Lending)
entries.summary: Describes higher interest rates charged by lenders who disregard the charge of usury, the social consequences, and advice for building a character who is an Usurer, including recommended Flaws and the Profession: Accountant Ability.
quotes: might ask closer to 50% interest on common loans

entries.title: Societas Merceris: the Pawnbrokers
entries.summary: A Redcap society that stores vis in distinctively shaped tokens; members may trade starting magic item levels for vis in their signature shape and receive a yearly pawn of vis from the House.
quotes: Pawnbroker Redcaps may trade two levels of their starting magic items for a pawn of vis in their signature shape

groups.title: The Church
groups.intro: The clergy, canon law, monastic life, orders and the Church in the saga.

entries.title: Magic and Sin (Saga Decision)
entries.summary: The core rules leave open whether magic is inherently sinful. This sidebar explains how each choice changes the relationship between magi, the Church, saints and angels, and what counts as penance.
quotes: If magic is inherently sinful, casting a spell is sinful no matter what the purpose.

entries.title: Hermetic Magic and the Sacraments
entries.summary: Describes the supernatural effects of the sacraments that magi can observe, such as baptismal names not serving as Sympathetic Connections and bodies that have received Extreme Unction being immune to magic for a few days.
quotes: a baptismal name cannot be used as a Sympathetic Connection to aid Penetration (unlike a birth name)
bodies that have received Extreme Unction cannot be affected by magic for three days

entries.title: Taking the Cross
entries.summary: Rules for a character committing to a Church-preached crusade: he gains an indulgence for outstanding penance and a temporary Faith Point, must fund his own travel and upkeep, and may at the troupe's discretion shed a Social Status Flaw.
quotes: He receives a single temporary Faith Point for the commitment

entries.title: Clergy as Player Characters
entries.summary: Clergy characters are built as ordinary grogs or companions under the standard character rules; the sidebar lists ways clergy can be tied into a covenant saga.

entries.title: Vows
entries.summary: Guidance on how to represent a Church character's vows at character creation: the Monastic Vows Story Flaw only if the troupe wants vow-driven stories, a suitable Personality Flaw or Regular otherwise, or simply a note with no Virtue or Flaw.

entries.title: Good Works
entries.summary: A season spent on charitable deeds, which for clergy may be a non-free season, giving experience in an appropriate Ability and a Faith Point.
quotes: Good works has a Source Quality of 2 in an appropriate Ability, and the character also gains 1 Faith Point.

entries.title: Recommended and Required Virtues, Flaws, and Abilities
entries.summary: A table of the Virtues and Flaws required and recommended, and the minimum Ability scores suggested, for popes, cardinals and archbishops; for bishops, abbots and senior officials; and for ordinary clergy.
quotes: Recommended Minimum Ability Scores: Artes Liberales 1, Church Lore 5, Civil and Canon Law 5, Dead Language: Latin 5, Theology 3.

entries.title: Election of the Bishop
